explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The LORD says, “Heed the rod and the One who ordained it.” So the call has two parts, the rod and the One behind it. The same verse says it is sound wisdom to fear His name, and I'd say that's worth listening to.

I get why that one tempts you, friend. Micah is a prophet, and the word of the LORD came to him (Micah 1:1). But the line itself doesn't mention prophets. It says, “Heed the rod and the One who ordained it.” The LORD points them to the One behind the rod.

Elders at the gate would make a nice scene, but they aren't in this verse. The LORD calls out to the city and says, “Heed the rod and the One who ordained it.” That's the whole instruction. Sometimes the answer is just the second half of the sentence, friend.

Careful, friend, because this one is a question and it points the other way. When the LORD asks, “Can I forget any longer, O house of the wicked, the treasures of wickedness and the short ephah, which is accursed?”, He is not saying He's ready to let it go. A few verses later He says, “Therefore I am striking you severely, to ruin you because of your sins.” (Micah 6:13) That is not a God who's dropping it.

Right, baker. He asks, “Can I forget any longer, O house of the wicked, the treasures of wickedness and the short ephah, which is accursed?” That is not a shrug. It's a question that says He has not forgotten. He then follows it with, “Therefore I am striking you severely, to ruin you because of your sins.” (Micah 6:13)

You got it, baker. The LORD asks, “Can I excuse dishonest scales or bags of false weights?” Think of a scale that cheats a little every single time. It's the kind of thing you'd never want near your cookie box. Back in verse 10 He also names the short ephah, which is accursed.

Those are fair things to worry about in business, but the LORD doesn't name them here. He asks, “Can I excuse dishonest scales or bags of false weights?” It's the tools of the trade that are crooked. Loans and wages aren't in the verse.

That's a serious list, friend, but it isn't the one in this verse. The LORD asks, “Can I excuse dishonest scales or bags of false weights?” He's talking about the equipment for measuring and weighing. Bribes and stolen land don't come up here.

That's the one, baker. The LORD says, “For the wealthy of the city are full of violence, and its residents speak lies…” Just before this, He mentioned the treasures of wickedness (Micah 6:10). Heavy words, friend, and He doesn't soften them.

Priests are a reasonable guess, but they aren't named in this verse. The LORD says, “For the wealthy of the city are full of violence…” That's the group He points to. Stick to who the text names, friend.

Violence makes you think of soldiers, I know. But the verse doesn't say that. The LORD says, “For the wealthy of the city are full of violence, and its residents speak lies…” The wealthy are the ones named.

Yes, friend. The LORD says the city's residents “…speak lies; their tongues are deceitful in their mouths.” That fits with the dishonest scales, because crooked words and crooked weights go together. It's one more charge in verse 12, right beside the violence.

The text says the opposite, baker. The LORD says, “…its residents speak lies; their tongues are deceitful in their mouths.” That's plain in verse 12. So this one is True, and it sits right next to the charge about violence.

Right, baker. The LORD says, “Therefore I am striking you severely, to ruin you because of your sins.” That word “Therefore” ties it back to the cheating and the lies in the verses before. This is a heavy part, friend, and I won't pretend it isn't.
No enemies in this verse, friend. The LORD says, “Therefore I am striking you severely, to ruin you because of your sins.” The reason He gives is their own sins. Enemies don't come up.
No bill collector in this verse, baker. The LORD says, “Therefore I am striking you severely, to ruin you because of your sins.” Sins are the reason the verse gives, not debts.

That's the catch, baker. The LORD says, “You will eat but not be satisfied, and your hunger will remain with you.” Imagine sitting down to a full plate and still feeling empty after. It's the first of several things He lists, and none of them are easy to hear.

Being sick isn't what the verse says, friend. The LORD says, “You will eat but not be satisfied, and your hunger will remain with you.” The problem is that the eating doesn't fill them. The hunger stays.

Sharing isn't in this verse, baker. The LORD says, “You will eat but not be satisfied, and your hunger will remain with you.” The catch is that they eat and still stay hungry. Look at the second half of that line, friend.
Not quite, friend. The LORD says, “What you acquire, you will not preserve; and what you save, I will give to the sword.” So whatever they save, they won't keep it. This one is False.
That's right, baker. The LORD says, “What you acquire, you will not preserve; and what you save, I will give to the sword.” So the saving doesn't hold up. Nothing they stash away stays with them.
You got it, baker. The LORD says, “You will sow but not reap…” That's sowing with no reaping to follow. If I did that with my dough, I'd just stare at a cold oven.
Watering isn't mentioned, friend. The LORD says, “You will sow but not reap…” The missing piece is the harvest itself. Nothing in the verse says the field goes dry.
Selling seed isn't in the picture, baker. The LORD says, “You will sow but not reap…” The seed goes into the ground and the harvest never comes in. Selling doesn't come into it.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, “you will press olives but not anoint yourselves with oil…” They do all the pressing, and the oil still doesn't end up on them. It's the same pattern as sowing but not reaping, earlier in the same verse.
That's the one, friend. The LORD says, “you will tread grapes but not drink the wine.” They do the treading and never get the drinking. Three times in one verse, and the pattern is clear.
Milk is a fine thing, baker, but it isn't in this verse. The LORD talks about pressing olives and treading grapes. The olives lead to oil and the grapes lead to wine. Milk never shows up.

Sweet guess, friend, but honey isn't in this verse. The LORD says they will press olives but not anoint themselves with oil. Honey isn't pressed from anything in the passage. Check what's being pressed and trod, and the answer follows.

Water makes sense for a thirsty crowd, baker, but it's not what the verse says. The LORD says they will tread grapes but not drink the wine. Grapes lead to wine here, not water. The verse sticks to what the work should have produced.

explanations.answer: Kept them and followed their counsel
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Micah 6:16 says the city kept those statutes and followed that counsel. Omri did evil in the sight of the LORD (1 Kings 16:25), and so did his son Ahab (1 Kings 16:30). So the city was walking a road those two had already laid out.

explanations.answer: Torn them down and burned them
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. Micah 6:16 has no tearing down and no burning in it. It says the city kept the statutes and followed the counsel. Omri and his son Ahab each did evil in the sight of the LORD (1 Kings 16:25, 30), so holding on to their ways was no small thing.

I wish that were so, baker, but verse 16 says otherwise. The city kept those practices and followed that counsel, so nothing had slipped its mind. Ahab reigned in the place of his father Omri (1 Kings 16:28), and the city was still following the ways of both. Those old habits were very much alive.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, “you will bear the scorn of the nations.” It comes right after He says He will make the city a desolation and its inhabitants an object of contempt. This is a heavy ending, friend. But the passage isn't the whole book, and Micah isn't finished.
Tribute is a good guess, friend, but the verse doesn't say it. The LORD says, “you will bear the scorn of the nations.” What they carry is scorn. No payment is mentioned.
Idols aren't in this verse, baker. The LORD says, “you will bear the scorn of the nations.” Scorn is what the city bears from them. Idols never come up.
